skills.name: Use the laws of indices, including zero, negative and fractional indices

note.text:
Laws of indices (same base a):
• aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ   • aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ   • (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
• a⁰ = 1 (a ≠ 0)   • a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, so 2⁻³ = 1/8
• a^(1/n) is the nth root of a: 8^(1/3) = 2
• a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)ᵐ: 8^(2/3) = 2² = 4. Take the root first, then the power.
On a phone we write a^(2/3) for a to the power two-thirds.

sections.heading: Index notation
sections.text:
{pw(2, 5)} means {2} × {2} × {2} × {2} × {2}: the base is {2} and the index (power) is {5}.
When you multiply powers of the same base, you are just counting how many times the base appears: {pw(2, 3)} × {pw(2, 2)} = ({2} × {2} × {2}) × ({2} × {2}) = {pw(2, 5)}. So add the indices.
Dividing cancels: {pw(2, 5)} ÷ {pw(2, 2)} = {pw(2, 3)}. So subtract. A power of a power multiplies: ({pw(2, 3)}){sup(2)} = {pw(2, 6)}.

sections.heading: Zero and negative indices
sections.text:
Keep dividing by {2}: {pw(2, 3)} = {8}, {pw(2, 2)} = {4}, {pw(2, 1)} = {2}, then {pw(2, 0)} = {1}, and next {2}⁻{sup(1)} = {frac(1, 2)}, {2}⁻{sup(2)} = {frac(1, 4)}.
So any number (except {0}) to the power zero is {1}, and a negative index means one over: a⁻ⁿ = {1}/aⁿ.
A negative index never makes the answer negative.

sections.heading: Fractional indices
sections.text:
Since a^({1}/{2}) × a^({1}/{2}) = a¹ = a, the index {1}/{2} means the square root. Similarly a^({1}/{3}) is the cube root.
For a^(m/n), take the nth root first, then raise to the power m:
{27}^({2}/{3}) = (cube root of {27})² = {3}² = {9}.
Taking the root first keeps the numbers small.

key_words.meaning: the small number showing how many times the base is multiplied
one over a number: the reciprocal of {4} is {frac(1, 4)}

mistake.why: A negative index means one over the power. The answer is a small positive fraction.

steps: The denominator {q} means the cube root: the cube root of {N} is {r}.
The numerator {p} means square it: {r}² = {r ^ p}.

cards.idea: Multiplying powers of the same base: add the indices.
A negative index means one over: a⁻ⁿ = {1}/aⁿ.
A fractional index is a root: the bottom of the fraction is the root, the top is the power.

misconceptions.explain: A fractional index is a root and a power, not a multiplication.
The denominator {q} means a root: take the root before the power.

solution: Root first: the {q == 2 ? 'square' : q == 3 ? 'cube' : 'fourth'} root of {r ^ q} is {r}.

misconceptions.explain: Multiplying powers adds the indices; multiplying the indices is for a power of a power.
x × x is x², not {2}x: there is no number in front.
Subtract indices when dividing; here we multiply, so add.

solution: Same base: add the indices, {a} + {b} = {a + b}.

questions.prompt: Evaluate {a}⁻{sup(n)}. Give the answer as a fraction.

misconceptions.explain: A negative index does not make the number negative: it means one over.

solution: A negative index means one over: {a}⁻{sup(n)} = {1}/{a}{sup(n)}.

misconceptions.explain: A fractional index is a root and a power, not a multiplication.
The denominator {q} means a root: take the root before the power.

solution: Root first: the {q == 2 ? 'square' : q == 3 ? 'cube' : 'fourth'} root of {r ^ q} is {r}.

misconceptions.explain: Adding indices is for multiplying powers; a power of a power multiplies them.
({pw('x', a)}){sup(b)} means {pw('x', a)} multiplied by itself {b} times, not {b} × {pw('x', a)}.
Multiply the indices: {a} × {b}, not {a} to the power {b}.

solution: A power of a power: multiply the indices, {a} × {b} = {a * b}.

where: a * b - d != a + b - d
